title: What Should School Demand of Its Students?
author: Lead Time
summary: A school leader who recently moved from international schools in Asia to Queensland, Australia uses a canteen conversation with a student who had missed his entire term of English Literature for sporting commitments to interrogate a question schools rarely make explicit: what should school actually demand of a child's time? Drawing a direct contrast between the academically intense, lesson-protective culture of his previous international schools and Queensland's sport-saturated culture, the author is honest that his own children seem happier in the new environment even as he worries whether 'pressure and challenge are actually the same thing.' He grounds the tension in David Yeager's research on adolescent psychology, noting that from puberty onward young people become acutely sensitive to social status and peer belonging, which makes the choice between a literature lesson and 'pulling on a school shirt with your mates' far less irrational than adults often assume. Having previously solved this at his Kuala Lumpur school through formal 'elite competitor' agreements requiring minimum attendance and work-completion commitments, the author ultimately argues the decision about how much missed learning a school will tolerate is not one that should be left to individual teachers or students, but is properly 'a leadership matter' reflecting the school's stated values. The piece closes without resolving the dilemma, instead insisting that whatever balance a school strikes, it should be an explicit, honestly acknowledged institutional choice rather than an unexamined accumulation of individually reasonable exceptions.
points: The concrete case of a student missing an entire term of English Literature for sporting commitments turns an abstract debate about school priorities into a specific, quantifiable cost that forces the question of who should be accountable for the missed learning.

Citing David Yeager's research that adolescents become acutely sensitive to social status and peer belonging from puberty onward reframes a student's choice of sport over class as developmentally rational rather than a simple failure of priorities, changing how adults should respond to it.

The author's conclusion that the attendance-versus-opportunity tradeoff is 'a leadership matter' rather than something left to individual teachers or students argues for institutional accountability and explicit policy (like the 'elite competitor' attendance agreements he used previously) over ad hoc, teacher-by-teacher exceptions.
quotes: He also mentioned, almost in passing, that because of all the competitions, he had yet to attend his English Literature class at all yet this term.

Having over a decade in high-performing international schools where academic achievement carried considerable weight, expectations from students and parents were incredibly high. But generally, we protected lessons pretty fiercely.
The problem comes when we expect our curriculum to somehow absorb the difference.
'Elite competitor' agreements set up that the students and parents had to sign that included minimum attendance and work completion commitments.
Given this, choosing between another English Literature lesson or pulling on a school shirt with your mates makes even more sense.
I'm increasingly convinced that the final decision is part of a school's job. This is a leadership matter. A decision about the philosophy and values of the school.
But I do think we should at least be honest that a choice has been made.
